opening.headline: Learn how to create specific, measurable success criteria and evaluation sets that resemble real-world use so you can tell if changing your prompts has improved things.
body: After changing the prompt, I read some examples and it looked good, but other examples seemed to have gotten worse. How should I judge this? Without standards, impressions become feel-based evaluations instead of evaluations, and as changes pile up, it becomes difficult to know what's better and what's worse.

In this class, we will look at the characteristics that a good success standard must have, and check in what order and with what data an evaluation set to measure the standard is created. Next, we follow the flow of grading one line of the evaluation set, and explain with examples why the numbers become meaningless when the evaluation set deviates from the actual usage distribution.

visual.alt: A scene where the answers to prompts v1 and v2 are placed side by side and it is not possible to decide which is better.
labels: How many days does delivery take?
How can I say it has improved?

paragraphs: Fixed prompt in customer inquiry chatbot. After reading some examples, I feel like the answers to the new prompt are better. However, when I open another example, the answer seems to have gotten worse. There is no basis to judge which side is correct.

In these situations, since there are no standards, the viewer's impression takes the place of evaluation. This is a feeling-based assessment. Each person feels differently, and even the same person feels differently depending on the day. As you make more and more changes, you become less able to explain which changes worked.

To improve, you must first decide what it means to get better. The question we will address in this class is how we can judge that something has improved. The answer is a set of success criteria and a set of assessments to be graded against those criteria.

callout.label: question of the day
callout.text: What can we say about the improvement after changing the prompt?

screens.outro: First, let's think about how we compared before and after the change so far.

screens.title: How do you compare before and after changes?
screens.lead: How do you compare before and after changes? When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about it in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: Have you tried running both versions with the same input?
items.answer: If you run two versions with different inputs, you won't know whether the differences are due to the change or the input. A comparison is only valid if both versions are run on the same set of inputs. This set of inputs is the evaluation set.

items.prompt: Have you written down the criteria for good in numbers or specific words?
items.answer: The standards in your head fluctuate over time. If you write it down, you can compare before and after changes based on the same criteria, and you can share the same criteria with your team members. If numbers are difficult, it is better to set a specific scale that can be applied consistently.

items.prompt: What happens when there are no standards?
items.answer: Without standards, there is no improvement. Every time you change, you judge it based on your impressions, so the changes for the better and the changes for the worse get mixed up. The first part of this class is how to set standards, and the second part is how to create data to be graded based on those standards.

screens.outro: Now that we've established why we need criteria, let's start by looking at the characteristics that a good success criterion should have.

screens.title: Success Criteria: Be Specific and Measurable
screens.lead: The table below compares the four properties of good success criteria with bad and good examples. Read each line, looking at what the bad example is lacking.

data.caption: Nature of Good Success Criteria
rows: specific
Clearly define what you want to achieve
good performance
Accurate emotional classification
measurable
Use quantitative indicators or consistently applicable scales
safe output
Out of 10,000 attempts, less than 0.1% of the output was caught by the harmfulness filter.
achievable
Base your goals on industry benchmarks, previous experiments, and expert knowledge
Unrealistic goals that exceed current model capabilities
Target number based on previous experiment results
relevance
Tailored to the purpose of the application and user needs
Only measure response length regardless of purpose
Medical apps focus on citation accuracy, everyday chatbots focus on response tone.
common mistakes
Write down your goal in one word and get it done
Accurate and natural answers
More than 95% of answers contain essential information in the first sentence
inspection questions
Is it possible to compare before and after changes in the same way based on this standard?
Pass if you feel better
Compare the percentage of criteria exceeded in the same set of inputs
data.notes: Citation accuracy is very important in medical apps, but may be less important in everyday conversational chatbots. Even topics as vague as ethics or safety can be translated into numbers, like the measurable examples in this table. Most use cases require a multidimensional assessment that looks at multiple criteria together rather than just one. When writing down the criteria, make a final check to see if you can compare before and after changes in the same way, as shown in the last row of the table. All good examples of tables have something in common: they are written so that no matter who calculates them, the same results are obtained. So comparisons before and after changes are unwavering.

screens.outro: Now that we have established a standard, let's take a step-by-step look at how to create an evaluation set to measure this standard.

screens.title: Evaluation set composition and representativeness
screens.lead: The following steps demonstrate a five-step workflow for creating and utilizing an assessment set. Select the right arrow to go through the steps one by one.

visual.alt: Illustration of an evaluation workflow that cycles through five steps, from goal definition to continuous evaluation.
labels: Enrich new cases from operational logs

steps.title: Step 1: Define your goals
steps.body: Decide what you want to make good. The success criteria established earlier are the result of this step. If your goals are vague, you cannot decide what data to collect or what indicators to use in later stages.

steps.title: Step 2: Data collection
steps.body: Gather input and expected results for evaluation. The evaluation should resemble the actual task distribution and should include a combination of borderline and adversarial cases as well as normal cases. You can write them yourself, have them created by domain experts, or pull them from operational data and historical logs.

steps.title: Step 3: Define Metrics
steps.body: Decide how you will score each question. If possible, design questions so they can be scored automatically. These include methods such as multiple choice, string matching, code scoring, and model scoring.

steps.title: Step 4: Run and Compare
steps.body: Compare the numbers by running the prompt before and after the change using the same evaluation set. Because the same evaluation set is used, changes in numbers are read as the effect of change.

steps.title: Step 5: Continuous evaluation
steps.body: An evaluation set is not created once and finished. Boundary cases and errors revealed during operation are continuously added to the evaluation set. If you accumulate logs, you can find good evaluation cases there.

steps.title: balance of quantity and quality
steps.body: The more questions you have, the better. A principle of assessment design is that a large number of items that can be scored automatically, even if the signal is slightly weak, is better than a small number of high-quality items that are scored by hand. However, many questions are meaningless if they do not resemble the actual distribution.

screens.outro: Now that we've established the workflow, let's take a look at the structure of how a single line of an evaluation set is actually scored.

screens.title: Flow of grading a line of evaluation set
screens.lead: If you select a number marker, you can see a detailed description of each cell in the evaluation set from input to grading result. Please select them in order starting from number 1.

visual.alt: A horizontal pipeline in which a line of evaluation sets passes through input, model output, baseline answers, and indicators and is judged as passing or failing.

markers.label: input
markers.title: input
markers.body: This is the first part of one line of the evaluation set. Contains questions or requests that real users might send. The evaluation is meaningful only if the input resembles the actual task distribution. For example, if it is a customer inquiry chatbot, it uses questions similar to actual inquiry sentences.

markers.label: model output
markers.title: model output
markers.body: This is the result created by the model receiving input. The prompts before and after the change respectively populate this field. Since we are comparing the output of two versions side by side from the same input, the premise of the comparison is that the inputs are the same.

markers.label: standard answer
markers.title: standard answer
markers.body: The other half of a line in the evaluation set, which is the expected result for the input. It may be the correct sentence, or it may be a key phrase that must be included. An evaluation set is completed only when the input and expected results are together.

markers.label: indicators
markers.title: Indicators and Decisions
markers.body: Metrics are rules that compare model output to a baseline answer to give a pass, fail, or numerical value. For example, a summary evaluation may establish criteria such as ROUGE-L of 0.40 or higher and consistency of 80% or higher in 1000 reference summaries. If you use the same evaluation set before and after the change, the change in value is the effect of the change.

markers.label: management
markers.title: How to grow your evaluation set
markers.body: OpenAI's Datasets are a way to add data to the dashboard, and we recommend using it as a dynamic space that continues to increase evaluation data over time. The idea is to add rows whenever you see edge cases or missed parts.

screens.outro: Now that we have confirmed the structure, we will explain with an example how the numbers become distorted when the evaluation set is biased.

screens.title: Case Commentary: Why Biased Evaluation Sets Make Numbers Meaningless
screens.lead: The instructor explains how numbers can be misleading when the evaluation set differs from the actual usage distribution. Select the right arrow to follow the point where the numbers deviate.

visual.alt: A bar graph comparing the question length distribution of the evaluation set and the question length distribution of actual traffic side by side.

steps.title: situation
steps.body: 90% of the evaluation set is short and easy questions. However, real users send us a lot of long questions. The distribution of the evaluation set and the actual traffic are different.

steps.title: Stage 1: Numbers have risen
steps.body: When I ran the evaluation set with the new prompt, the number rose to 92 points. If you look at the numbers alone, the change is a success. Just look at these numbers and see what happens when you deploy them in the next steps.

steps.title: Step 2: The part on the right is an easy question
steps.body: If we break down the reasons for the increase in numbers by question, most of them are improvements in short and easy questions. 90% of the evaluation set is of this type, so the overall number moves easily.

steps.title: Step 3: Long questions actually make things worse
steps.body: When it comes to long questions, the new prompt actually produces worse answers, but since there are so few long questions in the evaluation set, it doesn't show up in the overall numbers.

steps.title: Stage 4: Numbers are up, but quality is down
steps.body: Many actual users send long questions, which leads to increased complaints after deployment. If the evaluation set does not resemble the actual distribution, the actual quality may decrease even if the number increases. This is the problem of lack of representation.

steps.title: Step 5: Reinforce from logs
steps.body: Find long questions and edge cases in operational logs and add them to the evaluation set. Then, when the same change is evaluated again, the numbers show the deterioration in the long question. This is why we continue to grow the evaluation set with operational data.

screens.outro: There are cases where not only the distribution of the evaluation set but also the indicator itself runs counter to the purpose, so let's look at an example.

screens.title: When the indicator is inconsistent with the purpose
screens.lead: Below is the evaluation plan for some apps. When you select a highlighted passage, you will see why the indicator is off target and a solution. Select the verses one by one.

data.text:
Purpose of the app: Accurately citing source documents in medical consultation responses.  
Indicator 1: average length of response.  
Indicator 2: General metrics like BLEU and perplexity.  
Indicator 3: Judgments are made solely based on automatic scoring results and no human verification is performed..

marks.note: The purpose is citation accuracy, but measuring only the length defeats the purpose. It should be replaced with an indicator that directly measures whether the citation matches the sentence in the source document. Length is simply an indicator that is easy to use because it can be easily measured regardless of the purpose.

marks.span: General metrics like BLEU and perplexity
marks.note: If I only use generic metrics, I might miss important qualities in my work. Define indicators that fit the task together, and leave general indicators as secondary. Even if the general metrics are high, there is no guarantee that they will meet the goals of your app.

marks.span: Judgments are made solely based on automatic scoring results and no human verification is performed.
marks.note: You can't trust the numbers unless you check how well the automated scoring results match human judgment. The automatic scoring results are calibrated by matching them with human evaluations, and human judgment is used in the numbers.

screens.outro: Now that we have checked the indicators, we will conclude by summarizing the key contents.

screens.title: Key points and reflection
screens.lead: Review the key points of this lesson on one screen. Read the paragraph below and proceed to the summary screen.

paragraphs: Without success criteria, there is no improvement. Good criteria are specific, measurable, achievable, and related to the purpose of the application. Most use cases require multidimensional evaluation using multiple criteria together.

The evaluation set consists of inputs and expected results, and the numbers are meaningful only when they resemble the actual usage distribution. It contains general cases, borderline cases, and adversarial cases, and continues to grow them into operational logs. Always use the same evaluation set to compare before and after changes.

Lastly, you need to check whether the indicators match the purpose of the app and whether the automatic scoring results match human judgment. Since numbers are numbers that replace the purpose, I always look back to see if the numbers have strayed from the purpose.

checks.intro: Check for yourself what you just learned. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: Put your assessment workflow in the right order.
checks.explain: First decide what needs to be done well, have appropriate data and indicators, then implement and compare, and continue to evaluate thereafter.

checks.intro: Check for yourself what you just learned. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: 90% of the evaluation set is short and easy questions. Although the new prompt's ratings went up, actual users ended up asking longer questions and becoming more frustrated. What causes it?
options: Setting the evaluation index in numbers is itself a mistake.
The evaluation set did not resemble the actual task distribution, so the deterioration of long questions was not revealed.
The signal became weak due to the large number of items in the evaluation set.
The numbers could not rise because people did not directly evaluate them.
checks.explain: The evaluation set must resemble the actual distribution for the numbers to be meaningful. Longer questions and boundary cases should be augmented in operational logs.

wrong.0: Measurable criteria are needed, and the issue is the representativeness of the evaluation set.
wrong.2: Having a large number of questions is not a problem; having many questions that can be automatically evaluated is actually advantageous.
wrong.3: The cause is not whether a person is being evaluated, but rather how the evaluation data is structured.

checks.incorrectFeedback: Unfortunately, this is not the correct answer.

glossary.def: This is a goal that is specific and measurable. This serves as the basis for judging whether or not there is improvement.
It is a collection of evaluation data consisting of inputs and expected results.
This property indicates how much the evaluation set resembles the actual usage distribution.
It is a method of judging based on the impression that something is going well without any standards.

misconceptions.myth: Once you create the evaluation set, you are done.
misconceptions.fact: We need to continue to grow by adding borderline cases and errors revealed in operations. If you keep a log, you can find good evaluation examples there.

misconceptions.myth: If the number rises, it has improved.
misconceptions.fact: If the evaluation set is different from the actual distribution, the actual quality may decrease while the value increases. The meaning of the numbers depends on the representativeness of the evaluation set.

misconceptions.myth: It is better if the questions are at least of high quality.
misconceptions.fact: The assessment design principle is that a large number of items that can be automatically scored, even if the signal is slightly weak, is better than a small number of items that can be scored by hand.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: There is no improvement without success criteria.
Good standards are specific and measurable.
The evaluation set should resemble the actual usage distribution and include edge cases.
Compare using the same evaluation set before and after changes.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for your own reflection only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: If you were to write a measurable standard for the success of your app in one sentence, what would it be?
